summary: A durable requirement with an ID and acceptance criteria.
detail: A spec is AIDA's durable record of intent: what should exist, why it matters, and how completion is recognized. Its stable ID lets code, commits, tests, and history point back to the same requirement.
examples: BUG-14: show an explicit onboarding commit command
when_to_use: Whenever an idea, change, bug, or decision needs to survive beyond the current conversation.
best_when: The desired outcome and evidence of completion can be stated clearly.
cons: requires capture discipline
can become stale if not maintained

summary: Labels that describe the scale and purpose of a requirement.
detail: AIDA uses EPIC for a strategic container, STORY for user-visible behavior, TASK for bounded work, BUG for incorrect behavior, and functional or domain prefixes such as FR, VIS, PRIN, and ADR for specific requirement families.
when_to_use: When deciding how to frame a new piece of work or project knowledge.
best_when: The type matches the scope and audience of the requirement.
cons: misclassification creates confusing workflow expectations

summary: The lifecycle state of a requirement.
detail: Common states include draft, approved, queued, in-progress, completed, rejected, and blocked. Status describes where the requirement is in the workflow; it does not replace evidence that the code works.
when_to_use: When handing work between seats or explaining why a requirement is not yet complete.
best_when: State transitions reflect evidence and authority rather than optimism.
cons: status alone does not prove the implementation works

summary: Observable conditions that define when a requirement is done.
detail: Acceptance criteria turn intent into checks an implementer and verifier can agree on. Good criteria are concrete enough to test and specific enough to prevent two people from interpreting completion differently.

summary: Turning an idea, bug, or decision into a durable AIDA requirement.
detail: Capture is the point where an idea leaves conversation and enters the project memory. The result should name the intent, type, priority, acceptance, and useful relationships.

summary: A relationship that places focused work under a larger requirement or goal.
detail: A parent link gives a story, task, or bug its planning context. It prevents otherwise valid work from becoming orphaned and lets the graph show how a concrete change contributes to a larger outcome.

summary: Checking whether a requirement is clear and implementable.
detail: Evaluation looks for vague descriptions, missing acceptance, unsuitable types, absent priority, and orphaned work. It is a quality gate before work is queued or handed to an implementer.
examples: a readiness score flags an orphaned story before queueing
when_to_use: Before queueing or dispatching work that someone else will implement.
best_when: The cost of a bad handoff is higher than the cost of a short intake review.
cons: a readiness pass is not a design decision
can report warnings that direct work does not need

summary: A non-mutating readiness check before implementation or queueing.
detail: A dryrun scores a requirement across deterministic readiness dimensions and reports blockers without implementing anything. It helps the advisor fix intake quality before work reaches a doer.

summary: A role-specific worklist for routing approved work to a doer.
detail: A queue separates deciding what should happen from doing the work. A producer routes a requirement to a role; the consumer picks it up, works it, and marks it done.
examples: a dialog seat routes STORY-58 to the implementer queue
when_to_use: When one seat decides what should happen and another seat should do the work later.
best_when: Work is ready enough to hand off and the receiving role is known.
cons: adds ceremony for tiny local changes
stale queues hide real priorities

summary: An orchestrated pass that works an approved queue toward completion.
detail: A drain repeatedly selects eligible work, dispatches an implementer, reviews the result, and advances the queue. Human-required decisions remain visible instead of being silently guessed.
examples: an orchestrator drains approved implementer work until a review or design fork appears
when_to_use: For a bounded batch of already-approved work with clear handoff and review rules.
best_when: The queue is healthy and human-required decisions have an explicit route.
cons: must stop at meaningful ambiguity
poor intake quality scales into more noise

summary: Checking observable project state against a requirement or exercise.
detail: Verification compares the workspace, AIDA state, command evidence, and git history with the expected result. In this tutor, passing state is automatically recorded when the interactive exercise menu opens.
examples: a review checks acceptance and trace comments
when_to_use: After implementation or whenever you need evidence that a requirement's observable state is present.
best_when: The acceptance criteria identify facts a read-only check can observe.
cons: cannot judge ambiguous intent
some verification needs command evidence or human review

summary: A fresh inspection that checks implementation against acceptance and linked specs.
detail: Review is the handoff quality gate after implementation. It checks the code, tests, traceability, acceptance, and process artifacts before the requirement is treated as complete.

summary: The requirement ID in a commit message that closes the history loop.
detail: A commit such as `[AI:codex] feat(greet): add --upper flag (FR-1)` connects the change to its requirement in git history. Together with a trace comment, it keeps implementation provenance close to the code.

summary: A source-code comment linking an implementation back to a spec.
detail: A trace comment such as `# trace:FR-1 | ai:codex` travels with the code and makes the code-to-spec relationship searchable. It records which requirement the nearby implementation fulfills.

summary: A read-only check that compares project state with an expected result.
detail: A verifier inspects files, commands, git history, and AIDA state. A passing result means the observable work is present; it is evidence, not a replacement for the requirement itself.

summary: The decision or execution position a person or agent is occupying.
detail: A seat is the operational context behind a role: dialog decides and routes, advisor governs readiness and trade-offs, implementer changes code, and reviewer checks the result.
examples: entering the implementer role before picking up queued work
when_to_use: When multiple people or agents share a project and authority must be explicit.
best_when: The role's decision rights and handoff expectations are understood.
cons: role ceremony can slow a one-person experiment

summary: The seat that captures intent and routes work toward a decision.
detail: Dialog is the conversational intake seat. It clarifies what is wanted, captures the requirement, and sends ready work toward the advisor or implementer rather than letting intent disappear in chat.

summary: The seat that governs readiness, trade-offs, and human-required decisions.
detail: The advisor protects the quality of the queue and resolves design forks, approvals, and uncertainty. Automation can prepare work, but advisor authority is the boundary for consequential decisions.

summary: The seat responsible for changing code to satisfy an approved requirement.
detail: Implementers pick up routed work, make traceable changes, run verification, and hand the result back for review. They should not quietly redefine the requirement while coding.

summary: The seat that checks whether an implementation is ready to merge or release.
detail: Reviewers inspect the change with fresh eyes, compare it to acceptance, check tests and traceability, and surface gaps before completion is recorded.

summary: The project-local canonical history of requirements and events.
detail: The AIDA Store holds requirement objects, comments, relationships, and audit history. In distributed mode it lives on the `aida-store` branch in a linked `.aida-store/` worktree, with a rebuildable cache for fast reads.

summary: A rebuildable local index that makes AIDA reads fast.
detail: The SQLite cache accelerates queries over the canonical store. It is disposable: if it becomes stale or damaged, rebuild it from the store rather than treating the cache as the source of truth.

summary: A branch with independent history used to carry the requirement store.
detail: The `aida-store` orphan branch keeps requirement history separate from the code branch while remaining versioned and synchronizable. Its linked worktree exposes the canonical objects to the project.

summary: An isolated checkout where scoped work can happen safely.
detail: A session worktree is a sibling checkout on its own branch. It lets focused work proceed without disturbing the primary checkout, while AIDA tracks the lease and eventual release.
examples: a review branch in a sibling checkout
when_to_use: When work needs isolation from the primary checkout or a separate store history.
best_when: Changes can be scoped to a branch and should not disturb another active effort.
cons: extra directories and leases to understand
paths must be kept straight

summary: A scoped unit of work with a branch, worktree, and lease.
detail: A session gives focused work an explicit owner and boundary. Start creates the scope, work happens in its worktree, and end releases the lease without erasing the useful branch history.

summary: The ownership record that says who holds a scoped work session.
detail: A lease prevents two actors from assuming they own the same session scope. It makes active work visible and gives session end a precise thing to release.

summary: A reusable instruction package that teaches an agent how to perform a workflow.
detail: A skill packages purpose, routing, constraints, and procedure for an agent. It is executable project knowledge rather than a loose prompt, and it should point back to the requirements it serves.
when_to_use: When a workflow should be reusable across projects or agents.
best_when: The procedure, safety boundaries, and required outputs are stable enough to package.
cons: instructions can drift
too-broad skills become hard to follow

summary: Generated project files that connect an agent or tool to AIDA.
detail: A scaffold may include skills, hooks, settings, commands, or agent metadata. It makes a project discoverable to a tool, but it is not itself the project’s requirement source of truth.
when_to_use: When connecting a project to an agent or tool for the first time.
best_when: Generated files are reviewed and the AIDA store remains the canonical source of truth.
cons: generated files can become stale
unselected scaffolds can create ambiguity

summary: The connected path from intent through implementation to evidence and closure.
detail: A workflow is more than a command sequence: it defines who acts, what state changes, what evidence is required, and where a human must decide. AIDA keeps those transitions visible.

summary: A corroborated standby mode that auto-resolves safe confirmations but pauses on design forks.
detail: Zen reduces ceremony for mechanical confirmations while preserving the advisor’s place at meaningful design decisions. It is not permission to guess through ambiguity or bypass human authority.
examples: zen auto-resolves a confirmation but pauses at a design fork
when_to_use: When an orchestrated session needs less ceremony without losing human control over consequential choices.
best_when: Confirmation prompts are mechanical and design forks are explicitly marked.
cons: requires corroborated authority
never substitutes for a design decision
